title: Operator briefing — what to know right now
subtitle: What matters now if you run voice, SMS, or chat AI that talks to customers and gets work done.
disclaimer: Operational briefing · Not legal advice · Confirm against primary sources.

items.blurb: If you call cell phones with an AI voice, treat it like a robocall. You generally need written consent first, and the caller ID has to be honest.
Don't pretend the bot is a person, and don't oversell what the AI can do. That is already an FTC issue, not a future one.
Washington is talking about overriding state AI laws. That talk has not wiped out the state rules below — keep following them.
If a chatbot talks to Maine customers and could pass as a person, tell them it is AI. Text and voice both count.
If a bot is trying to sell something online (or influence a vote), say it is a bot. Don't let people think they are talking to a person.
If you or a customer use AI in hiring for California workers, employment AI rules already apply. Less relevant for day-to-day customer-service bots.

By 2027, if AI is making significant decisions about people — not just chatting — they get notice, a way to opt out, and a right to see what happened. Check whether any customer workflow is actually deciding, not just helping.
A customer-service chatbot bill for larger companies is sitting with the governor (sent Sept 14). Not law yet — watch whether it is signed or vetoed.
In a week, Connecticut starts treating automated decision tools more seriously. Using AI is not a shield if the outcome discriminates.

A year later, new automated decision tools will need to tell people they are talking to AI and give written notice before a decision. More of a hiring-tool issue than a pure customer-service voice bot issue.
In 2027, automated decisions that matter — including whether someone gets a lease — come with extra duties. Important if bots help with property leasing.
Texas already has a statewide AI law. Some uses are banned, and the attorney general can go after companies that develop or offer AI in the state.
If a Utah customer asks whether they are talking to AI, tell them. Some regulated jobs need you to say it up front.
If anyone uses AI on video interviews of Illinois candidates, they need notice and consent. Not a day-to-day customer-service bot rule.
If AI is used to hire in New York City, it needs a bias audit and the candidate has to be told. Hiring-adjacent, not a customer-service bot rule.
